Create a structured interview question set for hiring a [job title]. The key skills I'm evaluating: [list 4-5 skills — e.g., "writing ability, project management, client communication, self-direction, technical SEO knowledge"].
For each skill, give me: (1) 2 behavioral questions ("Tell me about a time when..."), (2) 1 situational question ("What would you do if..."), (3) What a great answer looks like (green flags), (4) What a bad answer looks like (red flags). Also include: 2 culture-fit questions specific to my environment (I value [describe: e.g., "autonomy, speed, direct communication"]), and 1 "closer" question that reveals their genuine interest in the role. Format this as an interviewer's scorecard I can print and use.

Create a client offboarding document template for when I complete a [type of project] for a client. Include these sections: (1) Project summary — what was delivered, (2) All deliverables with links/file locations, (3) Access & credentials handed over (checklist), (4) Maintenance notes — what needs ongoing attention and how to handle it, (5) Recommended next steps — what I'd suggest they do next, (6) Support terms — what's covered post-project and for how long, (7) How to re-engage — if they want to work together again, here's how. Make it professional and thorough — the kind of thing that makes a client think "I need to hire this person again."

Write 3 versions of a candidate rejection email:
1. After application review (no interview): Short, respectful, doesn't ghost them. Acknowledge they applied and wish them well.
2. After first interview: Warmer — mention something specific about the conversation (use placeholder [specific positive thing they said/did]). Explain it was competitive and we went with someone whose [specific qualification] was a closer fit. Leave the door open.
3. After final round (close runner-up): Genuinely personal. Acknowledge how far they got in the process. Be honest that it was a hard decision. Offer to stay in touch for future roles and mean it. Optionally offer brief feedback.
All under 100 words each. Tone: human, not corporate HR boilerplate. Getting rejected sucks — don't make it worse.
